title: Pre-Questions and the Attention Advantage
author: Sol in the Wild
summary: This practitioner article argues that pre-questions before reading do more than prime prior knowledge — they create what the author calls an 'attention advantage' that fundamentally changes how students engage with texts. Grounded in the Modal Model of Memory, the author explains that attention is the mechanism by which information passes from sensory memory into working memory, and that without it, even well-explained content fails to encode. When students receive 3-5 concrete, often numerical pre-questions before a FASE reading, they begin the text with a specific target and a personal investment in their own estimate, which shifts reading from passive completion to active scanning. The 'cognitive friction' of discovering one's estimate was wrong — 'I thought it was 15, but it was 7' — appears to strengthen encoding beyond simply receiving the correct answer. Student assessment data comparing matched content with and without pre-questions shows measurable retention differences attributable to the attentional mechanism. The author's key conclusion is that the question is no longer whether pre-questions work but how to design them with sufficient intentionality to maximise attentional focus at the moments it matters most.
points: Pre-questions reframe reading from passive completion to active information-seeking: because students don't know precisely where the answer will appear, they read with heightened vigilance throughout, inducing broad attentional engagement rather than selective skimming.

The cognitive friction of a wrong estimate — finding out that the correct answer differed from one's prediction — appears to strengthen memory encoding beyond simply receiving the correct answer, creating a contrast effect that makes the information stick.

Pre-questions compound two evidence-based learning mechanisms simultaneously: activating prior knowledge through retrieval of estimates and directing selective attention toward specific informational targets, multiplying their impact on encoding.

The technique has effectively zero implementation cost — 3-5 concrete questions tied to actual text content, answered on mini whiteboards before reading — making adoption a question of professional will rather than resource or time availability.

Student assessment data comparing the same concept with and without pre-questions shows a measurable retention gap that the author attributes to the attentional mechanism rather than topic interest or other confounds.
quotes: Before getting into pre-questions, it's worth grounding this in core idea: attention is the gatekeeper of learning.

Information from the environment first hits sensory memory. From there, only a small portion moves into working memory and the mechanism that determines what gets through is attention. If students don't attend to information, it doesn't matter how well it's explained or how important or relevant it is. It simply doesn't enter working memory in a usable way.

As students move through the FASE text, they're tasked with finding the answers to the pre-questions by underlining or highlighting the relevant information and updating their estimates on their whiteboards. That simple move changes how they approached the text. Because now, they're looking for something.
Students aren't passively moving through the text. They're actively scanning, tracking, and checking. They read more carefully around key details because they don't want to miss the answer.

In the days that follow, during retrieval practice, discussions, and assessments, the information tied to those pre-questions tends to stick more than information not explicitly connected to the questions. Students often remember both the correct answer and their original estimate. That contrast seems to matter.
Realizing I thought it was 15, but it was actually 7 creates a kind of cognitive friction that seems to strengthen their memory.
They move reading from something students complete to something they pursue. And if attention is the gatekeeper of learning, that's not a small impact.
